title.text: Words as numbers: bag of words, TF-IDF, embeddings and distance

objects.text: How can a computer find the right clause or policy when I describe it in plain words?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 4 of 14
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes: Welcome back. Last time you measured a model with a confusion matrix, precision, recall and a threshold, and every example was a table of numbers. Most business data is words, and a computer only handles numbers. Today text becomes numbers too. We build it slowly: first a list of numbers called a vector, from three friends rating two films; then four ways to say how close two vectors are; then three ways to turn a message into a vector. The question for today is on the screen.

slides.notes:
That question breaks into three things you can do by the end. You can explain a vector as a list of numbers and as an arrow, and work out its length, the dot product and cosine similarity with a pencil. You can follow how a message becomes a vector: first word counts, then TF-IDF weights, then an embedding.

And you can read the result of a semantic search and say where it would help or hurt in your own work.

title.text:
Your two hours: from film ratings to a
search that understands a description

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_7828579e.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: The search results are recorded in advance. You can ask me to run any description of yours live.

slides.notes:
Here is how the two hours run. The ideas take fifty-five minutes this time, because each measure is built one step at a time. We start with three friends rating two films, turn their ratings into vectors, and work out four ways of measuring closeness. Then we turn text into vectors in three steps: word counts, TF-IDF weights and embeddings.

A fifteen-minute demonstration shows a semantic search on three kinds of text. After the break you work the measures out by hand for fifteen minutes, and we finish with fifteen minutes on your own work.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  Why can accuracy mislead when the thing you look for is rare?
2.  What do precision and recall each ask?
3.  What happens when you lower the threshold?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png
objects.alt: Three questions

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 3. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. Why can accuracy mislead when the thing you look for is rare? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. A model that always predicts the majority class scores very high and catches nothing. In our run, always saying on time scored 90.8 percent. Ask for the baseline, precision and recall.

Question two. What do precision and recall each ask? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. Precision: of the cases flagged, how many were real, TP divided by TP plus FP. Recall: of the real cases, how many were flagged, TP divided by TP plus FN.

Question three. What happens when you lower the threshold? Think about your own work as you answer.

A good answer is this. The model flags more cases. It catches more real ones (true positives) and also raises more false positives.

If an answer was missing, last session’s take-away sheet or workbook page has it. Now to today.

How today connects: what we
already have and what it feeds

So where does today sit in the story? The dots along the top are the fifteen sessions, from the map at Session 0 to your plan at Session 14, and the gold one is today.

We already hold a picture as a list of numbers from Session 1 and k-NN: distance between houses from Session 2. Nothing today starts from zero.

What today adds is this: vectors, dot product, cosine, TF-IDF, embeddings.

And it feeds straight into what comes next. Session 5: how a language model uses those numbers. Keep that chain in mind, because each idea you learn today is a step on it.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: A list of numbers in a fixed order, such as Ana's two film ratings (3, 4). Each position is a dimension. Drawn as an arrow from 0.
A score from −1 to 1 for how closely two vectors point the same way: the dot product divided by both lengths.
A message as a vector of word counts, one dimension for each word in the vocabulary. The word order is lost.
Term frequency times inverse document frequency: a word count weighted so that rare words count more than common ones.
A vector, produced by a trained model, whose numbers place texts with similar meanings close together.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Vector. A list of numbers in a fixed order, such as Ana's two film ratings (3, 4). Each position is a dimension. Drawn as an arrow from 0.

Cosine similarity. A score from −1 to 1 for how closely two vectors point the same way: the dot product divided by both lengths.

Bag of words. A message as a vector of word counts, one dimension for each word in the vocabulary. The word order is lost.

TF-IDF. Term frequency times inverse document frequency: a word count weighted so that rare words count more than common ones.

Embedding. A vector, produced by a trained model, whose numbers place texts with similar meanings close together.

Keep those words close. The first idea uses them straight away, so let us begin.

title.text:
Words must become numbers before
a computer can compare them

objects.text: Session 3 measured numbers. A search compares a plain question with every clause, and both are words.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_grid_0.70.png
objects.alt: grid

objects.text: First: how close are two lists of numbers?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_calculator_0.70.png
objects.alt: calculator

objects.text: Then: three ways to turn a message into a list.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.70.png
objects.alt: magnifier

objects.text: Last: find a clause from a plain description.

slides.notes:
Those five words are the whole session, and here is why we need them now. In Session 3 everything we measured was already a number: a score from 0 to 1, a count of right and wrong answers. Today's question is about words. A manager types a plain question, and the computer must find the contract clause that answers it, so it has to compare words with words.

A computer can only compare numbers. So we go in three steps. First, lists of numbers, and four ways to say how close two lists are, on an example with no words at all. Then, three ways to turn a message into such a list. Last, the search itself. The first step starts with something everyone knows: film ratings.

title.text:
A vector is a list of numbers in a
fixed order: Ana rates two films

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_list_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A vector is a list of numbers in a fixed order: Ana rates two films

objects.text: Ana rates Film 1, a comedy, 3 out of 10, and Film 2, an action film, 4.

runs.text: Written as a vector: (3, 4).
Chloe gives 4 and 3: the vector (4, 3), a different vector.
Each position is a dimension.

slides.notes:
Film ratings have no words in them, so we can learn the tools before we need them for text. The first of today's five words was vector, so let us build one. Ana gives a comedy 3 out of 10 and an action film 4. Write the two numbers side by side in brackets, comedy first, and you have the vector three, four.

A vector is a list of numbers in a fixed order. The order matters: Chloe gives the comedy 4 and the action film 3, so Chloe's vector is four, three. Same numbers, different vector, different taste. Each position in the list is called a dimension, so these vectors have two dimensions.

You have met vectors before: the house in Session 2 was floor area and distance to town, and the picture in Session 1 was a list of 64 numbers.

title.text:
Draw a vector as an arrow from 0: across
by the first number, up by the second

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_arrow_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Draw a vector as an arrow from 0: across by the first number, up by the second

objects.text: Three friends rate the same two films.

runs.text: The direction of the arrow shows the mix of tastes.
Its length shows how strongly the person rates.
Ben points the same way as Ana, twice as long.

slides.notes:
A list of two numbers can also be drawn, and the picture will carry the rest of the session. On squared paper, start at zero, go across by the first number and up by the second, and draw an arrow to that point. For Ana: three across, four up.

Ben rates six and eight. Each of Ben's numbers is Ana's times two, so Ben's arrow points in exactly the same direction and is twice as long. Ben has the same mix of tastes as Ana and simply rates more generously. Chloe, four and three, leans the other way, towards the comedy.

So an arrow has two things: a direction, which is the mix, and a length, which is how strong. Keep both in mind, because the measures that follow treat them differently.

title.text:
Session 2's two distances on the
film arrows: Chloe is closer to Ana

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_recall_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Session 2's two distances on the film arrows: Chloe is closer to Ana

objects.text: As in Session 2: Euclidean is the straight line, Manhattan the walk along the grid. Smaller is closer.

slides.notes:
With arrows on paper, we can ask who has a taste closest to Ana, and you already have two tools from Session 2. Euclidean distance is the straight line between the two tips: square each gap, add, take the square root. Manhattan distance walks along the grid: add the gaps.

From Ana to Ben the gaps are 3 and 4. Nine plus sixteen is twenty-five, and the square root of twenty-five is five; the grid walk is seven. From Ana to Chloe the gaps are 1 and 1, so the square root of two, about 1.41, and a walk of two.

Both distances say Chloe is closer to Ana. Yet Ben has exactly Ana's mix of tastes. Distance mixes direction and length together, so we need a measure that looks at direction.

title.text:
The dot product multiplies
matching ratings and adds them

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_dot_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: The dot product multiplies matching ratings and adds them

objects.text: Worked first, then the formula. A bigger dot product means the two lists agree more.

slides.notes:
The first step towards direction is a score of agreement, called the dot product. Two people agree when they rate the same films high, so multiply the matching ratings and add. Ana with Ben: three times six is eighteen, four times eight is thirty-two, and eighteen plus thirty-two is fifty.

Ana with Chloe: three times four is twelve, four times three is twelve, total twenty-four. Now the formula, read aloud: a dot b equals a one b one plus a two b two. Here a is Ana's list and b is Ben's; a one is Ana's Film 1 rating, b one is Ben's, and writing them side by side means multiply.

For longer lists we write a capital sigma, which means add up, one term for each position i. You met this in Session 1: a weighted sum is a dot product.

title.text:
Read a dot product: big when both rate the
same films high, 0 when nothing is shared

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_dotread_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Read a dot product: big when both rate the same films high, 0 when nothing is shared

objects.text: The dot product grows with agreement, and also with length.

runs.text: Same mix: 50.
One rates only comedy, the other only action: 0.
Ana with herself scores 25, with Ben 50: long arrows win.

slides.notes:
Fifty and twenty-four are only numbers until we know how to read them, so here are three cases. On the left, Ana and Ben like the same mix, and the score is a big fifty. In the middle, one person rates only the comedy, five and zero, and the other only the action film, zero and five.

Five times zero plus zero times five is zero. Nothing shared gives a dot product of zero, and you will see that zero again with text. On the right is the weakness. Ana with herself scores nine plus sixteen, twenty-five. Ana with Ben scores fifty. Ben agrees with Ana more than Ana agrees with herself, only because Ben's arrow is longer.

To remove that effect we first need the length of an arrow.

title.text:
The length of an arrow: square each
number, add, then take the square root

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_length_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: The length of an arrow: square each number, add, then take the square root

objects.text: As in Session 2, Pythagoras's rule for a right-angled triangle: sides 3 and 4 give a long side of 5.

slides.notes:
To measure an arrow, look at the triangle it makes on the paper: three across, four up, and the arrow as the long side, the same right-angled triangle as Session 2's straight-line distance. Pythagoras's rule says the long side is found by squaring the two short sides, adding, and taking the square root.

Squaring means a number times itself, so three squared is nine and four squared is sixteen. Nine plus sixteen is twenty-five. The square root is the number that times itself gives twenty-five, which is five. So Ana's arrow is five long. Ben: thirty-six plus sixty-four is one hundred, square root ten, twice Ana's, as the picture showed.

Chloe: sixteen plus nine, also five. The formula writes the length of a between double bars. It is the Euclidean distance from zero to the tip.

title.text:
An angle measures the turn between two directions,
and its cosine scores it between 1 and minus 1

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_angle_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: An angle measures the turn between two directions, and its cosine scores it between 1 and minus 1

objects.text: A right angle is 90°, a half turn 180°. A calculator's cos key gives the cosine of an angle.

slides.notes:
We now have lengths, and the other half of an arrow is its direction. The gap between two directions is an angle, measured in degrees. Arrows that point the same way have an angle of zero. Ana and Chloe are sixteen degrees apart. A right angle, ninety degrees, is the corner of a page: the nothing-shared case from the dot product slide.

A half turn, one hundred and eighty degrees, is opposite directions. Mathematicians score an angle with its cosine, a number your calculator gives with the cos key. The cosine of zero degrees is one. Of sixteen degrees, zero point nine six. Of ninety degrees, zero. Of one hundred and eighty, minus one.

So one means same direction, zero means unrelated, and minus one means opposite. How do we get that score from two lists of ratings?

title.text:
Cosine similarity divides the dot product
by both lengths, so only the angle is left

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_cosine_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Cosine similarity divides the dot product by both lengths, so only the angle is left

objects.text: Ana and Ben point the same way: 1.00. Chloe is 16° away: 0.96.

slides.notes:
The answer uses the two pieces we just built. Take the dot product and divide it by the two lengths multiplied together. Ana with Ben: the dot product was fifty, the lengths five and ten, five times ten is fifty, and fifty divided by fifty is one. One means the same direction, as the picture shows.

Ana with Chloe: twenty-four divided by five times five, which is twenty-four over twenty-five, zero point nine six. That is the cosine of sixteen degrees, the angle you saw. Now the formula, in words: cos theta equals a dot b divided by the length of a times the length of b.

Theta, the Greek letter, names the angle. This score is called cosine similarity, and bigger means closer. Some tools report cosine distance, which is one minus it.

title.text:
Cosine similarity ignores length:
doubling every rating leaves it at 1

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_scale_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Cosine similarity ignores length: doubling every rating leaves it at 1

objects.text: Length cancels out, so cosine compares only the mix.

runs.text: Ben doubles Ana: dot product and lengths both double.
For text: a short note and a long report on one topic point the same way.
That is why cosine is widely used for text.

slides.notes:
Why does dividing by the lengths fix the weakness we saw?

Compare Ana with herself and Ana with Ben. Ana with Ana: dot product twenty-five, lengths five times five, twenty-five; twenty-five divided by twenty-five is one. Ana with Ben: Ben doubles every rating, so the dot product doubles to fifty, but Ben's length doubles too, five times ten is fifty, and the two cancel.

Cosine is one again. Cosine similarity looks at the mix and ignores how strong it is. For text this is usually what we want. A one-line note and a three-page report about late deliveries have very different lengths, yet they are about the same thing, so they should point the same way.

title.text:
The four measures can pick different
winners, so ask which one a tool uses

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_compare4_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: The four measures can pick different winners, so ask which one a tool uses

objects.text: Every cell can be redone with a pencil. None is wrong: each measures something different.

slides.notes:
You now have four measures, so let me put them side by side on one question: who is closer to Ana, Ben or Chloe?

Euclidean distance: five against 1.41, so Chloe. Manhattan distance: seven against two, Chloe again. For both, smaller is closer. The dot product: fifty against twenty-four, so Ben, partly because Ben's arrow is long. Cosine similarity: one against zero point nine six, so Ben, because Ben points exactly Ana's way.

They disagree, and none of them is wrong. The two distances see length and direction, the dot product rewards length, and cosine sees direction only. When a vendor says similarity, ask which measure. All of this was ratings, though. Our real question is about words.

title.text:
Text has no numbers yet: three
ways to turn a message into a vector

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_c60e5827.png
objects.alt: Text has no numbers yet: three ways to turn a message into a vector

objects.text: Each step fixes a weakness of the one before. The comparing stays the same: today's measures.

slides.notes:
Our question was how a computer can find the right clause from a plain description, and the four measures only work on lists of numbers. A message is words. So the rest of the ideas turn a message into a vector, in three steps that each fix a weakness of the one before.

First we count words: that is called a bag of words. Then we weight the counts so that rare words count more: that is TF-IDF. Then we let a trained model produce numbers for meaning: that is an embedding. At the end, the comparing is exactly what you just learned, mostly cosine similarity.

Let us start with counting, on messages small enough to do by hand.

title.text:
A bag of words counts each word: three
tiny messages become three vectors

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_bowhand_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: A bag of words counts each word: three tiny messages become three vectors

objects.text: Invented messages. The vocabulary decides the dimensions: one per word.

slides.notes:
Here are three tiny messages: send the invoice; the invoice is late; the rice is late. Step one: list every word that appears, once each. There are six: send, the, invoice, is, late, rice. That list is called the vocabulary, and each word in it becomes one dimension.

Step two: for each message, count how often each word appears. The invoice is late has no send, one the, one invoice, one is, one late and no rice, so it becomes the vector zero, one, one, one, one, zero. Six numbers, like Ana's two, only longer. This is called a bag of words, because it is like tipping the words into a bag: the counts survive and the order is lost. Dog bites man and man bites dog get the same counts.

title.text:
On word counts, filler words such
as “the” and “is” push the score up

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_bowcos_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: On word counts, filler words such as “the” and “is” push the score up

objects.text: Two of the three words S2 and S3 share, “the” and “is”, say nothing about the topic.

runs.text: S2 with S3: cosine 0.75.
S2 with S1: cosine 0.58.
Every word counts the same.

slides.notes:
Now the counts are vectors, so cosine similarity works on them exactly as on the films. This is the closeness score from 0 to 1 that Session 2 promised, before the rare-word weights we add next; counts are never negative, so it never goes below 0. Take the middle message, the invoice is late.

With send the invoice it shares two words, the and invoice, so the dot product is two. Its length is the square root of four ones, two; the other's is the square root of three, 1.73. Two over two times 1.73 is 0.58. With the rice is late it shares three words, the, is and late, so the dot product is three, both lengths are two, and three over four is 0.75.

Two of the three shared words are the and is, which say nothing about the topic. We need weights.

title.text:
Two counts for every word: tf in one
message, and df across all the messages

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_df_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Two counts for every word: tf in one message, and df across all the messages

objects.text: M06, one of 40 invented customer messages, asks for a corrected invoice for jerrycans of oil.

runs.text: tf, term frequency: invoice appears twice in M06.
df, document frequency: invoice is in 4 of the 40.
A rare word points to its message.

slides.notes:
To weight words we need a larger set of messages, so we use the forty invented Nile Valley Foods customer messages from Session 2. Message M06 is a customer saying invoice 2305 shows the wrong price for each jerrycan of cooking oil and asking for a corrected invoice.

For every word we count two things. Term frequency, tf, is how many times the word appears in this message: invoice appears twice. Document frequency, df, is how many of the forty messages contain the word at all: the is in twenty-two, invoice in four, jerrycan in only one.

A word that is in almost every message tells you nothing about which message you are reading. A word in very few points straight at its message. Rare words should weigh more.

title.text:
Inverse document frequency turns rare
into heavy: N ÷ df, softened by a log

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_log_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Inverse document frequency turns rare into heavy: N ÷ df, softened by a log

objects.text: idf = ln(N ÷ df). Inverse: df sits below the line, so the smaller df, the bigger the weight.

slides.notes:
How do we turn rare into heavy?

Divide the number of messages, N, forty, by the document frequency. Jerrycan, in one message: forty. The, in twenty-two: 1.8. But forty against 1.8 is too steep: one rare word would outweigh everything else. So we soften it with a logarithm. You met one in Session 2: log base 2 counted yes-or-no questions, the halvings from 8 down to 1.

The natural log, written l n, works the same way with a special number e, about 2.718: how many times you multiply by e to reach a value. The log of one is zero, of ten 2.30, of a hundred 4.61: multiplying by ten only adds 2.30. So forty becomes 3.69, 1.8 becomes 0.60, and the order is kept. That is the inverse document frequency.

title.text:
TF-IDF multiplies the two: tf ×
idf, worked for message M06

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_tfidf_text_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: TF-IDF multiplies the two: tf × idf, worked for message M06

objects.text: Textbook form, worked by hand. The recorded run used a smoothed form of the same idea.

slides.notes:
The weight of a word in a message is the two numbers multiplied: term frequency times inverse document frequency, which is where the name TF-IDF comes from. Jerrycan: one times 3.69, so 3.69. Invoice: it appears twice, so two times 2.30, which is 4.60, the highest. Oil: 1.90.

Send: 1.61. Please: 0.86. The: 0.60, the lowest. Invoice wins because it is both repeated and rare, and the, which appears everywhere, counts least. The formula in words: TF-IDF of term t in document d equals the count of t in d times the log of N over the number of documents containing t.

Here a document is one message and a term is one word. The bag of words gave every word the same weight; TF-IDF fixes that.

title.text:
The recorded run used scikit-learn's smoothed
form, then set each message to length 1

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_tfidf_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: The recorded run used scikit-learn's smoothed form, then set each message to length 1

objects.text: Recorded run, 6 Nov 2026: scikit-learn 1.9.1 TfidfVectorizer, default settings.

slides.notes:
Software rarely uses the textbook form exactly. Our recorded run used scikit-learn, a free Python library, with its default setting called smoothing. The inverse document frequency is the log of forty-one over one plus df, plus one. The extra ones act as if one more message held every word.

That avoids dividing by zero, and a word found in every message keeps a small weight. Then each message is divided by its length, the same square root of the sum of squares as Ana's arrow, here 18.54, so every message has length one. For invoice: two times 3.104 is 6.208, divided by 18.54 is 0.335.

The ranking is the same as the textbook form: invoice first. Session 2's nearest messages were found the same way: the cosine of two TF-IDF vectors.

title.text:
Counts cannot see meaning: a flood question
and the force majeure clause share no word

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_noshare_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Counts cannot see meaning: a flood question and the force majeure clause share no word

objects.text: Force majeure: a contract clause that excuses delays caused by events nobody controls.

runs.text: No shared word, so the dot product of the counts is 0, and the cosine 0.
TF-IDF only weights the words that are there.
We need numbers for meaning.

slides.notes:
Weighting helps, but it still counts words, and here is where counting fails. A manager asks: what happens if heavy rain floods the road and the delivery cannot get through?

The clause that answers it is force majeure, a contract clause that excuses delay caused by events nobody controls, such as a flood. Count the words. Floods and flood are different words to a counter, and delivery is not delay. They share no word at all. So, exactly as in the nothing-shared case of the dot product, the score is zero and the cosine is zero.

In the recorded run the keyword search found no shared word for this question. Yet a person sees at once that both are about a flood stopping a delivery. We need numbers that describe meaning.

title.text:
An embedding is a vector whose numbers
describe meaning: a toy with two dimensions

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_plane_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: An embedding is a vector whose numbers describe meaning: a toy with two dimensions

objects.text: A toy I made up: dimension 1 is how much a word is about money, dimension 2 about trucks.

runs.text: invoice and receipt: cosine 0.98.
invoice and lorry: cosine 0.47.
Close meaning, close direction.

slides.notes:
Numbers that describe meaning are called an embedding. To see the idea, here is a toy with two dimensions that I chose myself: how much a word is about money, and how much about trucks. Invoice is four and one, mostly money. Receipt is three and one and a half.

Lorry is one and four, mostly trucks. Now use the cosine you know. Invoice with receipt: the dot product is twelve plus 1.5, which is 13.5; the lengths are 4.12 and 3.35; the cosine is 0.98, almost the same direction. Invoice with lorry: four plus four is eight, divided by 4.12 times 4.12, about 0.47.

Close meaning, close direction. In a real embedding nobody chooses or names the dimensions. So where do the numbers come from?

title.text:
A trained network produces the numbers:
384 of them, learned from examples

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_network_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: A trained network produces the numbers: 384 of them, learned from examples

objects.text: Simplified. all-MiniLM-L6-v2, a small open model: text in, 384 numbers out, none with a name.

slides.notes:
Nobody writes these numbers by hand. A neural network reads the text and produces them, much like the digit network of Session 1, which read 64 numbers and produced 10 scores. Here a sentence goes in and 384 numbers come out, so the embedding has 384 dimensions. Other models use other sizes.

The network's weights were learned in training: according to its model card, this model was fine-tuned on more than a billion pairs of related sentences, so that sentences with similar meaning end up with vectors that point in similar directions. No single number means money or trucks; the meaning is spread across all 384.

That is a simplified account. So the numbers are learned from examples. Let me show you some real ones.

title.text:
A real embedding has 384 numbers:
nobody reads them, we compare them

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_numbers_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: A real embedding has 384 numbers: nobody reads them, we compare them

objects.text: Recorded run, 6 Nov 2026, all-MiniLM-L6-v2. Every vector has length 1. Gold: close in meaning.

slides.notes:
These are real numbers from our recorded run, the first eight of 384 for three texts: the flood question, the force majeure clause and the governing law clause, which says which country's law applies. Numbers can be negative or positive, and none of them can be read on its own.

As a last step, this model divides every vector by its length, so every vector has length one, as we did with TF-IDF. We compare them with cosine similarity, using all 384 numbers. The flood question and force majeure score 0.36. The question and governing law score 0.03, almost a right angle.

Word counts gave the flood question and force majeure zero; the embedding finds the link. Now let me run it as a search.

title.text:
Demonstration: describe a clause in
plain words and find its formal name

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_7.30x3.90_ac023c7a.png
objects.alt: Demonstration: describe a clause in plain words and find its formal name

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: The right term in the top three.
A keyword search that finds nothing.
Compare scores only within one search.

slides.notes:
Everything so far comes together in one tool, called semantic search: search by meaning. I type a plain description, and the computer returns the formal clause, term or paragraph that matches. Four steps. I describe it in plain words. The model turns my description into 384 numbers, an embedding.

It works out the cosine similarity with the embedding of each of ten passages. And it ranks them and shows the top three. Next to it I show a keyword search, which uses TF-IDF and so only sees shared words. You choose the kind of text: contract clauses, finance terms or HR policy paragraphs.

Watch for the right answer in the top three, and for the keyword search finding nothing at all.

title.text:
Contract clauses: the right clause came
first for all four plain descriptions

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_search_11.90x4.25_fb6098b1.png
objects.alt: Contract clauses: the right clause came first for all four plain descriptions

objects.text: Recorded run, 6 Nov 2026. Gold: the right clause. Scores: cosine similarity.

slides.notes:
What did you see? The right answer near the top, and a keyword search that sometimes found nothing. Here are the recorded results for contract clauses. On the left, four descriptions in plain words. What happens if heavy rain floods the road and the delivery cannot get through?

Force majeure first, at 0.36. Who pays us back if the supplier mistake costs us money?

Indemnity, a promise to cover the other side's losses, first. Can we walk away without giving a reason?

Termination for convenience. The contract keeps running every year unless we say something in time?

Automatic renewal. In the last column, the keyword search finds the right clause for three of the four, and for the flood question no clause shares a single word with the description.

title.text:
Finance terms: first once, in the top three
for three of four, so a person still chooses

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_search_11.90x4.25_a24ea585.png
objects.alt: Finance terms: first once, in the top three for three of four, so a person still chooses

objects.text: Recorded run, 6 Nov 2026. The right term was fourth for the second description.

slides.notes:
Clean results like that can mislead, so here is the same run on finance and invoice terms. This one is messier, and I show it on purpose. For the money we owe the maize miller, the right term, accounts payable, came second behind depreciation. For checking the order, the delivery and the bill before paying, three-way match came first.

For make sure our books match what the bank says, bank reconciliation came second, behind bad debt write-off. And for the shop that sent back damaged bags, the right term, credit note, came fourth, behind accounts receivable. That is a reasonable answer, because the shop does owe us money. Semantic search gives a shortlist, and a person picks from it.

title.text:
HR policy: the right paragraph was in the top three
for all four, and keyword search found none first

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_search_11.90x4.25_36806265.png
objects.alt: HR policy: the right paragraph was in the top three for all four, and keyword search found none first

objects.text: All 12 searches: right answer first 7, in the top three 11; keyword search first 4.

slides.notes:
That shortlist idea holds for the third kind of text, HR policy paragraphs. The person afraid to report a colleague who steals stock gets whistleblowing, first. The malaria message gets sick leave, first. The unhappy employee who wants to complain gets the disciplinary procedure first and the grievance procedure second.

The person who wants to quit gets the notice paragraph second. In all four the right paragraph is in the top three, and the keyword search never puts the right one first. Over all twelve searches: semantic search had the right answer first in seven and in the top three in eleven.

Keyword search had it first in four. Twelve searches on thirty short invented passages is a demonstration, and a small one.

title.text:
The four measures agree when every vector has
length 1, and can part ways when lengths differ

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_agree_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: The four measures agree when every vector has length 1, and can part ways when lengths differ

objects.text: This model divides every vector by its length as a last step. Skip that step and the measures split.

runs.text: Lengths left alone: Euclidean says bank reconciliation, the right term.
Dot product and cosine say bad debt write-off.
Check the top three, whichever measure.

slides.notes:
All that ranking used cosine similarity, so would another of our four measures change the winner?

With this model, mostly not. Every vector has length one, so the cosine is the dot product divided by one times one: the two are the same number. And the straight-line distance between two tips of length one shrinks exactly as the cosine grows, so it ranks the same way.

In our twelve searches all four agreed on the top answer in eleven. I can skip the last step and leave the lengths alone. For the books and bank question, the two candidate vectors then have lengths 4.49 and 5.34. Euclidean and Manhattan distance pick bank reconciliation, the right one.

The dot product and cosine pick bad debt write-off. Check the top three, whichever measure you use.

title.text:
Work out the four measures
by hand for three viewers

objects.text: 15 minutes
Hands-on, no computer
Fill in the table for the three pairs.

runs.text: Mark A, B and C on squared paper and draw the arrows.
Euclidean: √(gap₁² + gap₂²). Manhattan: gap₁ + gap₂.
Dot product: a₁b₁ + a₂b₂.
Length: √(a₁² + a₂²), given on the sheet.
Cosine: dot product ÷ (length × length).

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t04_blank_5.50x3.55.png
objects.alt: A table for three pairs of viewers and four measures, with the rating vectors and lengths above

objects.text: You keep: The twelve answers and which pair each measure calls closest.

slides.notes:
The ideas and the search used the same few calculations, and now it is your turn with a pencil. Take fifteen minutes; I walk round while you work. Three viewers rate two films out of ten: A gives three and four, B three and one, C six and zero.

Mark the three points on squared paper and draw an arrow from zero to each. For each pair, work out four numbers, in the same order as on the slides. Euclidean: square the two gaps, add, take the square root. Manhattan: add the gaps. Dot product: multiply matching ratings and add.

Cosine: divide the dot product by the two lengths, which are on the sheet: A five, B 3.16, C six. Then ask which pair each measure calls closest. They will not all agree.

title.text:
Where would semantic search
help or hurt in your own work?

objects.text: Write three plain descriptions of terms you use, then say where searching by meaning would help.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.80.png
objects.alt: magnifier

objects.text: Find by idea
Clauses, policies or terms you can describe but not name.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_doc_0.80.png
objects.alt: doc

objects.text: Match near copies
Duplicate invoices, supplier or customer names.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_folder_0.80.png
objects.alt: folder

objects.text: Group by topic
Enquiries or complaints sorted by what they are about.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_key_0.80.png
objects.alt: key

objects.text: Keep exact search
Codes, numbers and names must match exactly.
Three descriptions with predictions, your option, and the cost of a wrong first answer.

slides.notes:
You have worked the measures yourself, so now turn the idea on your own work. You have fifteen minutes, and I walk round. First, pick three formal terms you use, such as a clause or an account name. Write a plain description of each, using none of its words, as if explaining it to a new colleague.

Predict whether a keyword search would find it, and whether a semantic search would. Write yes, no or unsure. Then think of a pile of text you search today and choose one option: find by idea, match near copies, group by topic, or keep exact search, where an invoice number or a legal citation must match exactly.

Say aloud what a wrong first answer would cost you. If time allows, I run one description live on a few paragraphs of your own text.

Keep the cheat sheet, and try a plain
description on your own documents

objects.text: What you keep from today

How can a computer find the right clause or policy when I describe it in plain words?

Keep the cheat sheet. It has the four measures, the length of a vector and TF-IDF, each with its formula, every symbol named and the worked numbers from today. If a vendor says similarity or distance, ask which measure, and whether the vectors were set to length one first.

Try it this week: write a plain description of a clause or policy from your own documents and ask whether a keyword search would find it. Next time, Session 5, we see how a language model uses vectors like these to choose the next token.

We began with this question: How can a computer find the right clause or policy when I describe it in plain words? Before you go, say in one sentence what you can now say about it.
